text: Genetics tools are used in applied conservation management for taxonomic iden- tification, delineation of management units, management of wild populations, captive breeding and reintroduction and control of invasive species, disease and 2. To assess the extent to which genetic tools are being used for applied conserva- tion management, we conducted a systematic literature review of over 53,767 papers focussing on wildlife research that reported results on species delineation, translocations and population augmentation. We synthesised information on pa- pers that used genetics tools in an expressly applied manner across all wildlife 3. We found that the application of genetics tools in conservation management was biased towards fishes, mammals and birds and northern hemisphere locations, 4. Despite genetics tools being a highly published topic, it was difficult to find pub- lished applications of these tools in both the primary and the grey literature. Of the 115 papers on 152 species that could be considered an applied use of a genet- ics tool expressly for conservation management, only 49 had definable applied outcomes. The remaining 66 made recommendations, but it was often unclear if the recommendations were ever used to make conservation management deci- sions because of the time-lag between publication of the initial recommendation and publication of the results of the use of the tool in a conservation management situation, as well as the lack of dissemination in the primary literature.

text: Our study highlights the relative low publication rate of applications of genetics tools compared to the general conservation genetics field. These tools appear to have either a low percentage of translations into publication (‘conservation genetics publishing gap’) or a poor uptake among wildlife conservation managers (‘conservation genetics gap’)—the two are indistinguishable in this review.

text: 6. Policy implications. Conservation genetics tools must be brought to the forefront of conservation policy and management. Users should support the use of systems and accessible databases to increase the uptake of genetics tools for conservation The principal aim of conservation genetics is to develop strategies for biodiversity preservation through conserving the species ge- netic diversity (Pertoldi et al., 2007). Applying conservation genetics tools to conservation problems requires defined outcomes and man- agement decisions (Frankham et al., 2017). Applying conservation genetics tools to a conservation problem is not simply a genetic anal- ysis of populations with no direct applied conservation outcomes or interventions. In the academic literature, recommendations are often made concerning the use of a particular population genetics study for conservation purposes, however, the application of that recommendation into outcomes and management decisions is some- times difficult to discern. For instance, a paper by Leary et al. (1993) on bull trout Salvelinus confluentus examined the occurrence of ge- netic divergence and hybridisation in the species, and suggested considerations about the source of future translocated individuals.

text: If those considerations were used in any future translocation of that species, it is not necessarily clear from either the literature (Spruell Instead, truly applied conservation genetics goes beyond sug- gesting interventions to support conservation to applying the in- terventions and understanding their effectiveness. For example, applying the principles of conservation genetics and using these conservation genetics tools a priori allows for a more complete un- derstanding of populations and interventions, and the use of novel interventions to conserve the species. Some pertinent examples of this were the translocation of rescued yellow cardinals Gubernatrix cristata to their original source locations (Dominguez et al., 2019) and the evaluation of the long-term genetic management plan for black-footed ferrets Mustela nigripes (Wisely et al., 2003). However, the application of genetic analysis and tools post hoc is often used to understand the effects of an intervention rather than driving the in- tervention or future interventions. An example of this can be found in the Oklander et al., 2020 study of black and gold howler monkeys Alouatta caraya, where genetic analysis of origin of founders oc- curred after the translocation, but no future conservation interven- tion was evident from the results. Genetic assessment after captive breeding or translocation has occurred is also evident in studies of European sturgeon Acipenser sturio (Roques et al., 2018) and fishers Martes pennanti (Drew et al., 2003). These post hoc analyses can give valuable information for understanding the translocated pop- ulations, but in and of themselves do not use conservation genetics tools to their fullest potential. On the other hand, a large number of these post hoc analyses provide the most valuable sets of recom- mendations (e.g. Oliveira-Jr et al., 2016), providing the blueprint for future use of genetics tools for effective conservation interventions.

text: Conservation genetics as an applied science was at its infancy in 2010 (Frankham, 2010) when two large hurdles were suggested to be limiting its uptake—wildlife managers lacking genetics training and (unfounded) fears of outbreeding depression. Since then, the gap between genetics (or genomics) research and conservation ap- plications is still evident (Haig et al., 2016) but perhaps not as wide as sometimes thought (Garner et al., 2016). Since 2010, some new barriers to effective translation from research to conservation ap- plication have been suggested, ranging from conservation genetics publications not being valued by academia (Haig et al., 2016), mis- understanding of traditional genetics and genomics approaches (Garner et al., 2016), cost (Shafer et al., 2015), access to expertise and funding (Taft et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2017) and failure of aca- demic authors to explicitly link research to policy and conservation In this study, we conduct a systematic review of the conserva- tion genetics literature to identify studies where applied conserva- tion genetics tools have been directly used and evaluate if we could detect an actual applied outcome to the use of the tools. We seek to determine the extent of use of applied conservation genetics tools used directly in wildlife conservation as reported in the literature and gain an understanding of their directed, applied use. text: Specifically, that studies must concern the application of conserva- tion genetics tools to wildlife conservation interventions directly, in both in situ (wild) and ex situ (zoos or other captive breeding) situ- ations. This means that interventions such as translocation or spe- cies identification were directly impacted by the use of the genetic tool and were included, while other interventions, such as habitat protection, only tangentially use the product of the genetic tool, and were not included. The initial search resulted in 53,767 publica- tions, which were subsequently reviewed for relevance and repeats excluded. After applying these criteria, 472 publications from the initial search were further investigated at the abstract or full text level. Each paper was categorised as having either ‘recommenda- tions only’ or ‘successful application’ of conservation genetics tools.

text: The recommendations only category included papers where a con- servation genetics tool was used, but an actual applied on-ground outcome was not evident in either the paper or a further search of the grey literature (up to 2020). The successful application category included papers where a conservation genetics tool was used, and an applied, on-ground intervention occurred as a direct result of the data from the conservation genetics tool. For instance, the paper by Nash et al. (2018) used single nucleotide polymorphic markers (SNPs) to assign pangolin seizures from illegal trade to possible geographic sources based on known-origin pangolin samples. The paper then recommended the use of the tool to repatriate illegally traded pangolins and to explore the possibility of lineage-based tax- onomic units. As this paper was published in 2018, there is thus far no published evidence that either recommendation has been used; therefore, the paper is listed as ‘recommendation only’. Conversely, the paper by Morin et al. (2010) used mitochondrial genomes to determine that rather than one cosmopolitan orca species, the three ‘ecotypes’ should be elevated to full species. text: The majority of the applied conservation genetics interventions and recommendations found in this review were supplementation, rein- troduction, control of introduced species or hybrids and identifica- The analysis has shown that only the 0.09% of the total number of articles searched had an on-ground applied application/outcome from the use of conservation genetics tools. The papers that were excluded from the analysis (66 of the 115) used language in the abstract to indicate that they were using a conservation genetics tool with an applied outcome, but actually only made recommen- dations. For instance, Drew et al., 2003 indicate which population of fisher (Martes pennanti) would be the most appropriate source population for future translocations, but an exploration of the pub- lished and grey literature could not find evidence that the recom- mended population had been used for translocation. We believe that there are many potential reasons for the low number of arti- cles found to fit our criteria. First, the restricted nature of our cri- teria (i.e. publication in a source searchable by a free search engine) for an applied use of the genetics study meant that many applica- tions were ‘lost’ in reports and unpublished documents. Second, the time-lag between the genetics study and the publication of the application of that study to a conservation or management out- come (Christie et al., 2021), some as much as 16 years between recommendation and uptake (e.g. jaguar subspecies boundaries recommended in Eizirik et al., 2001 and applied in Kitchener et al., 2017). Third, the number of published studies could have been im- pacted by the difficulties researchers have in obtaining permits to work with endangered species which therefore impedes conserva- tion biologists and managers from applying conservation genetics to target species (Shirey & Lamberti, 2010). Fourth, the number of studies focused on the northern hemisphere and first world coun- tries reflects the lack of economic investment in most countries in the analysis and equipment necessary to conduct conservation genetics including the time-lag inherent between technologies be- coming common in first world countries (Torres-Florez et al., 2018).

Moreover, the known deficiencies in Google Scholar, a crawler-based search engine that tunes its first result page rather than seeking precision, probably contrib- uted the lack of trackability or follow-up of many recommendation Taylor et al. (2017) identified a ‘conservation genetics gap’, that is, the integration of genetics into conservation management, but we identify a ‘conservation genetics publishing gap’ that is indis- tinguishable from integration and uptake of conservation genetics tools. Rather than a lack of access or funding (at least in most devel- oped countries) to conservation genetics tools, management organ- isations face other, intrinsic, barriers to disseminating the results to other end users and interested parties. These barriers include lack of publication in peer-reviewed journals that are easily searchable using the most commonly available free search engines (Haddaway et al., 2015), lack of expertise to use the genetic information that is being supplied (Cook & Sgrò, 2019), or a lack of communication between managers and the scientific community (Taft et al., 2020). This study has shown that the apparent conservation genetics gap is growing wider as the number of papers that use applied conservation genet- ics or recommend the use of conservation genetics applications is relatively stable, while the number of papers that published in the broad arena of conservation genetics is steadily increasing.

text: Conservation genetics and the conservation genetics tools that are used to conserve wildlife populations have been in use since the second half of the 20th century (Hedrick & Miller, 1992). Even when genetics tools have lagged behind the conservation intervention they are meant to inform (e.g. translocation of puma Puma concolor from Texas and Central America to Florida to bolster Florida pan- ther P. c. coryi populations (Johnson et al., 2010; Saremi et al., 2019)), the subsequent analysis allows for retroactive understanding of the genetic consequences of the intervention. Our analysis shows that despite the increase over time in total papers published in the broad field of conservation genetics (Figure 2), there has not been a con- comitant increase in the peer-reviewed publication of applied inter- The lack of publication of the use of conservation genetics tools for the management of wildlife species is no longer due to a lack of research, training or guidelines. Rather, the lack appears to be due to a failure to disseminate the information, both failures and successes, in an easily accessible manner. This lack needs to be acknowledged and both managers and researchers need to ensure that genetic man- agement tools are incorporated in future research programs and that the results are disseminated in a manner such that other researchers and managers can easily access the information. When research using conservation genetics tools are conducted solely by academics, the information may never be seen by managers or may not address their specific questions (Merkle et al., 2019). When research using these tools are conducted solely by managers, the information may never be published in a manner available to other managers or researchers, or those who speak a language other than English, therefore increasing the conservation genetics gap (Taylor et al., 2017).

Use of conservation genetics tools has been part of the distinct field of applied conservation genetics for at least 30 years and is still a field in its infancy as indicated by its low publication rate, relative to the general conservation genetics field. These tools appear to have low percentage of translations into pub- lication rather than a poor uptake among wildlife conservation managers. It is recommended that an explicit repository of information about the use and implementation of conservation genetics tools be developed and updated in the manner of the Conservation Evidence Database (Sutherland et al., 2019), but rather than a ‘search and synthesis’ approach, the database would be updatable by the researchers—a user upload proce- Most instances of the use of conservation genetics tools found in this systematic review were geographically biased with studies concentrated in North America and western Europe and focussed mostly on fishes, mammals and birds. This geographic bias is well- known in the conservation literature but is probably more due to the limitation in languages and search engines than an actual bias in research or knowledge (Amano et al., 2021). To combat this bias, more funding must be allocated to publish conservation information, no matter what language, in easily accessible reposi- tories. The taxonomic bias is more insidious and probably based on societal preferences (Troudet et al., 2017). To combat this bias, again, more research funding must be allocated towards under- studied groups, especially invertebrates (Gordon et al., 2020).

text: There is limited use of applied conservation genetics tools for highly threatened or endangered species; most species used in studies are IUCN Least Concern. This issue appears to be a lack of funding for threatened species indicating the severe lack of resources available by governments towards the protection of biodiversity. Targeted global funding initiatives rather than gov- ernment funding strategies, which rely on the whims of political parties, need to be assessed as a means towards halting biodiver- sity declines (Scheele et al., 2018; Waldron et al., 2013).
